buckets.title: Magnetic fields and orientation reasoning
buckets.badge_reason: Three-dimensional page conventions and oriented surfaces must be explicit before quantitative magnetic laws can be introduced.

capabilities.action: Interpret magnetic-field direction from in-plane arrows and dot/cross page conventions.
capabilities.success_criterion: Identify one physical field direction consistently when the viewing convention changes.

capabilities.action: Compare how strongly a magnetic field passes through differently oriented surfaces.
capabilities.success_criterion: Rank surface orientations by through-going field without changing field strength or surface size.

capabilities.action: Distinguish a change in velocity direction from a change in speed for motion under a purely perpendicular magnetic force.
capabilities.success_criterion: Given successive velocity and force directions, explain why the path may curve while speed and kinetic energy remain unchanged.

microtopics.title: One magnetic direction, several page marks
microtopics.badge_reason: The learner must coordinate a three-dimensional axial direction with two-dimensional page marks before later magnetic rules are readable.
entry_assumptions: Can distinguish a location in a diagram from a direction assigned at that location.
microtopics.inferential_jump: Magnetic field B is an axial vector: its direction is tied to an oriented rotation convention, and dot/cross marks encode out-of-page and into-page directions rather than particle paths.

teaching_path.action: Fix the page convention before interpreting the drawing: a dot means toward the viewer and a cross means away from the viewer.
teaching_path.why_valid: The marks are projections of one directed quantity; declaring their viewing meaning first prevents a symbol from being mistaken for a physical object.
teaching_path.output: dot = toward viewer; cross = away from viewer

teaching_path.action: Turn the same physical setup so a direction that was drawn in the page now points toward the viewer, then redraw only its direction mark.
teaching_path.why_valid: Changing the viewpoint changes the page mark while leaving the physical direction fixed, so agreement across the two drawings tests interpretation rather than memorization.
teaching_path.output: same physical B: in-page arrow -> dot after the viewpoint turns

teaching_path.action: Trace one direction line around and through a bar magnet instead of stopping at a pole.
teaching_path.why_valid: A direction map must remain continuous; following the same line through the material exposes the error in treating the outside segment as an endpoint.
teaching_path.output: outside N -> S; inside S -> N; no endpoint

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Magnetic field lines begin at a north pole and end at a south pole everywhere.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: Trace one magnetic field line through and around a bar magnet. Where can it stop?
misconceptions.repair: Treat field lines as a direction map: they continue in closed loops, including through the magnet.

exit_task.prompt: A diagram shows one magnetic direction once as an arrow and once with a page mark after the view is changed. Explain how both can describe the same physical direction and say whether the associated direction line may terminate at a pole.

answer.summary: The page mark changes with the view, but the physical magnetic direction does not; a field-direction line is continued through the magnet rather than terminated at a pole.
reasoning: Bind every page mark to the declared viewing convention instead of reading dot or cross as an object.
Compare the physical direction before and after the viewpoint change; only its two-dimensional depiction has changed.
Continue the direction line through the magnet so the apparent outside endpoint is seen as part of a closed path.
answer.check: Rotate the imagined viewpoint back. The mark should recover the original arrow direction, and tracing the same line should never require an endpoint.

oracle.no_numeric_claim: The exit answer makes a directional classification and continuity argument; it asserts no computed numerical value.

microtopics.research_contribution: This author-created bridge from page notation to axial direction needs subject and pedagogical review before promotion.

predict.prompt: If an arrow that points toward you is redrawn after the page is turned, must the physical magnetic direction have changed?
predict.defensible_answer: No. The page symbol can change because the view changed while the physical direction in space stays fixed.

attempt.produces: A pair of sketches of the same magnetic direction from two viewpoints, plus one continuously traced line around and through a bar magnet.

rubric.criterion: The two sketches use the declared dot/cross meanings consistently.
rubric.evidence_of: Keeping physical direction separate from the mark used to display it.

rubric.criterion: The traced line continues through the magnet rather than ending at a pole.
rubric.evidence_of: Recognizing a field-line drawing as a continuous direction map.

accepted: The first view uses an in-plane arrow, the turned view uses the matching dot or cross, and the magnet sketch continues outside and inside without a terminal point.
rejected: A dot is labelled as a particle coming out of the magnet and the traced line is stopped at the south pole, so representation marks are treated as physical endpoints.

route.ask: Before reading the mark, which way is the viewer facing relative to the page?
route.why_this_ask: The convention cannot be interpreted until the viewing direction is fixed.

route.ask: If the object does not move but your view turns, what is allowed to change: the physical direction or only its page mark?
route.why_this_ask: This forces separation of the invariant direction from its depiction.

route.ask: Follow one marked direction line into the magnet. What would make it continue rather than stop?
route.why_this_ask: The learner must repair the apparent endpoint by tracing the same directional object.

reconstruct.differs_from_teaching_path: The declarative path states the convention then demonstrates invariance; the elicitation route makes the learner choose a viewpoint first and discover which feature can remain invariant.

boundary_test.prompt: If the same magnetic direction is exactly perpendicular to the page, can it still be shown by an ordinary in-plane arrow without changing the view?
boundary_test.answer: Not without losing the out-of-page information; that is precisely when the dot/cross convention carries information an in-plane arrow cannot.
boundary_test.confirms: The page convention represents a three-dimensional direction rather than decorating a two-dimensional sketch.

microtopics.title: Through-going field depends on surface orientation
microtopics.badge_reason: The hard move is treating the surface as oriented and comparing how much field passes through it without changing either its size or the field.
entry_assumptions: R1: magnetic field B is an axial directed quantity with explicit in-plane and out-of-plane representation conventions.
microtopics.inferential_jump: Magnetic flux measures the component of magnetic field through an oriented area; changing the surface orientation changes flux even when B and area size stay fixed.

teaching_path.action: Attach a normal arrow to the surface before comparing orientations, so the face has an explicit through-direction.
teaching_path.why_valid: A flat surface alone has no preferred side; the normal supplies the orientation needed to distinguish with-through from against-through.

teaching_path.action: Rotate the same loop from face-on to tilted to edge-on while leaving its size and the surrounding field unchanged.
teaching_path.why_valid: Only orientation changes, so any change in through-going field is attributable to how the surface faces the field rather than to a stronger field or larger loop.
teaching_path.output: face-on -> most through; tilted -> less through; edge-on -> none through

teaching_path.action: Keep the physical surface fixed but reverse which normal arrow is declared positive.
teaching_path.why_valid: Changing the chosen orientation reverses the sign convention while leaving the physical setup unchanged, separating signed description from apparatus.
teaching_path.output: normal one way -> one sign; reversed normal -> opposite sign

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Flux is just magnetic-field strength times area, so orientation does not matter.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: A loop with fixed area rotates from face-on to edge-on in a uniform field. What must happen to its flux?
misconceptions.repair: Project the oriented area along the field direction: the dot product selects the component through the surface.

exit_task.prompt: Three identical loops sit in the same uniform magnetic field: one face-on, one tilted, and one edge-on. Rank the amount of field passing through them and explain the role of the chosen surface normal.

answer.summary: The face-on loop has the greatest through-going field, the tilted loop has less, and the edge-on loop has none; the normal states which side counts as the positive orientation.
reasoning: The field strength and loop area are held fixed, so orientation is the only changing feature.
A face presented to the field admits the greatest through-going component, while an edge presented to it admits none.
Reversing the named normal changes the sign convention but not the physical loop or field.
answer.check: Imagine rotating only the loop continuously from face-on to edge-on; the ranking should change smoothly without any appeal to a stronger or weaker field.

oracle.no_numeric_claim: The exit answer ranks orientations and explains sign choice qualitatively; it contains no computed numerical result.

microtopics.research_contribution: This author-created orientation sequence makes the matrix's flux distinction teachable without asserting an ungated flux equation.

predict.prompt: If the field and loop size stay fixed, can simply turning the loop change how much field passes through its face?
predict.defensible_answer: Yes. Turning the loop changes how its oriented face meets the field even though neither magnitude nor area changes.

attempt.produces: Three sketches of the same loop at face-on, tilted, and edge-on orientations, each with a normal arrow and a qualitative through-going ranking.

rubric.criterion: Only orientation changes across the three sketches.
rubric.evidence_of: Isolating orientation as the cause of the changed through-going field.

rubric.criterion: Every sketch carries an explicit normal arrow.
rubric.evidence_of: Treating the surface as oriented rather than as an unsigned patch.

accepted: The same-sized loop is shown in all three cases, with face-on ranked above tilted and edge-on ranked at none, and every face has a declared normal.
rejected: The face-on case is drawn with a larger loop or stronger field, so the ranking can no longer be attributed to orientation alone.

route.ask: Which quantities are staying fixed while the loop is turned?
route.why_this_ask: The learner must isolate orientation before making a comparison.

route.ask: What arrow could you attach to the face so 'through this side' has a definite meaning?
route.why_this_ask: This elicits the need for an oriented surface before naming it.

route.ask: If you reverse only that arrow, what changed physically and what changed only in the description?
route.why_this_ask: It separates sign convention from the unchanged apparatus.

reconstruct.differs_from_teaching_path: The teaching path supplies a normal first; the elicitation route starts from an unexplained orientation effect and makes the learner invent the missing face-direction needed to describe it.

boundary_test.prompt: What happens to the through-going field when the loop is exactly edge-on to the field?
boundary_test.answer: It reaches the limiting case of none passing through the face even though the field itself remains present and unchanged.
boundary_test.confirms: The comparison depends on how the surface faces the field, not merely on field presence.

microtopics.title: A perpendicular magnetic force redirects without speeding up
microtopics.badge_reason: Learners often transfer the everyday rule 'force means speeding up' to a case where force is everywhere sideways to the instantaneous motion.
entry_assumptions: Can distinguish a velocity arrow's direction from its length.
Can recognize perpendicular directions and interpret a zero dot product geometrically.
microtopics.inferential_jump: When the magnetic force is perpendicular to the instantaneous velocity, it can continually turn the velocity arrow without lengthening or shortening it; the magnetic interaction redirects motion without supplying kinetic energy.

teaching_path.action: At one instant, draw the velocity arrow tangent to the path and the magnetic-force arrow perpendicular to it.
teaching_path.why_valid: The rung's claim applies to a pure magnetic interaction in the stated perpendicular case, so the local force-versus-velocity geometry must be fixed before any conclusion about speed is made.

teaching_path.action: Advance a short time step and redraw the velocity with a changed direction but the same arrow length, while keeping the force sideways to the new velocity.
teaching_path.why_valid: A sideways change alters direction while preserving the magnitude represented by arrow length; repeating that local update builds a curved path without a speed increase.

teaching_path.action: Use the dot-product check on the force and instantaneous velocity at each snapshot.
teaching_path.why_valid: Perpendicular vectors have zero dot product, so the magnetic force has no component along the motion to supply or remove kinetic energy.
teaching_path.output: F ⟂ v -> F·v = 0 -> magnetic contribution to speed change = 0

misconceptions.wrong_idea: A magnetic field makes a charged particle speed up simply because a force acts on it.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: A particle curves in a uniform pure magnetic field. If its speed rises, what interaction supplied the extra kinetic energy?
misconceptions.repair: Compare the force with the instantaneous velocity: a perpendicular magnetic force turns the motion, while its zero dot product with velocity means it does not add kinetic energy.

exit_task.prompt: A particle moves through a region where the only force is magnetic and is perpendicular to its instantaneous velocity. State what may change about the velocity and what must remain unchanged, and justify the answer with the force-velocity geometry.

answer.summary: The velocity direction may change, so the path can curve, but the speed and kinetic energy remain unchanged because the magnetic force has no component along the instantaneous motion.
reasoning: Read speed from the length of the velocity arrow and direction from where that arrow points.
A force perpendicular to the velocity changes the direction of the arrow rather than its length in the ideal pure-magnetic case.
The perpendicular force-velocity dot product is zero, which is the work-or-power check that no kinetic energy is transferred by the magnetic force.
answer.check: Compare two nearby snapshots: the tangent direction should rotate while the velocity-arrow length stays fixed and the force remains perpendicular to the local tangent.

oracle.no_numeric_claim: The exit answer distinguishes direction, speed, and kinetic-energy changes qualitatively; it computes no magnetic-force magnitude or trajectory radius.

microtopics.research_contribution: This author-created local-snapshot construction teaches the work-free redirection distinction without importing a quantitative Lorentz-force magnitude or circular-motion relation.

predict.prompt: A force is acting on a moving charge, but the force arrow is exactly sideways to the velocity arrow. Must the particle be getting faster?
predict.defensible_answer: No. A sideways force can change the direction of motion while leaving the speed unchanged.

attempt.produces: Two successive velocity-force snapshots on a curved path, with the velocity-arrow lengths compared and a force-velocity dot-product check.

rubric.criterion: The later velocity arrow changes direction without changing length.
The force is kept perpendicular to the instantaneous velocity and the dot-product check is identified as zero.
rubric.evidence_of: Connecting the geometry to the no-energy-transfer conclusion.

accepted: The path bends, the two velocity arrows have equal lengths, each force arrow is sideways to the local velocity, and the response uses the zero dot product to explain unchanged kinetic energy.
rejected: The later velocity arrow is longer solely because a force exists, even though the force is drawn perpendicular to the motion.

route.ask: Which feature of a velocity arrow represents speed, and which represents direction?
route.why_this_ask: The learner must separate the two properties before one can change without the other.

route.ask: If the force is exactly sideways, what could change about the velocity arrow without changing its length?
route.why_this_ask: This makes redirection the learner's construction rather than a stated rule.

route.ask: What does the dot product of two perpendicular arrows tell you here?
route.why_this_ask: The geometric check closes the work-or-power claim without asking for a force magnitude.

route.ask: If the field strength changed while the force stayed perpendicular, which conclusion survives?
route.why_this_ask: It tests the invariant distinction: curvature may change, but the pure magnetic interaction still does not supply kinetic energy.

reconstruct.differs_from_teaching_path: The teaching path starts from a declared perpendicular snapshot; the elicitation route first asks the learner to separate velocity length from direction, then makes the curved-path construction emerge from that distinction.

boundary_test.prompt: If an additional non-magnetic force has a component along the velocity, may the speed still be assumed constant?
boundary_test.answer: No. The no-speed-change conclusion belongs to the pure magnetic perpendicular-force case; an additional along-motion force can transfer kinetic energy.
boundary_test.confirms: The rung's conclusion is conditional on the stated force geometry and does not claim that every curved charged-particle path has constant speed.

teaching_routes.title: Completed magnetic-direction constructions
entry_needs: Learners can read ordinary arrows and compare orientations.
learner_actions: Explain why turning a surface changes through-going field while its size stays fixed.
Follow a completed two-snapshot construction showing direction change with unchanged velocity-arrow length.
help_plan: Keep the viewing convention beside every dot/cross mark.
Show the surface normal before asking for an orientation comparison.
Keep the force perpendicular to each instantaneous velocity and show the zero force-velocity dot-product check.
teaching_routes.reveal_plan: The declarative route reveals each completed distinction and its self-check.

source_preferences.reason: The authored source is the only authority claimed for these constructions.

when_not_suitable: Do not extend this route into Lorentz-force magnitude, induction, circular-orbit, or motional-emf calculations without governed relations.

teaching_routes.title: Elicit magnetic direction and orientation
entry_needs: Learners can commit to a direction or orientation prediction before seeing the construction.
learner_actions: Predict which page mark preserves one physical direction.
Construct a normal for a surface before ranking orientations.
Use boundary cases to test the distinction.
Predict whether a sideways magnetic force must increase speed, then reconstruct the local velocity change from two snapshots.
help_plan: Ask for the viewing direction before naming the symbol.
Ask what stayed fixed before revealing the orientation ranking.
Close every attempt with the model response and misconception repair.
Ask which part of a velocity arrow encodes speed before revealing the unchanged-length construction.
teaching_routes.reveal_plan: The tutor withholds the key distinction until the learner has made a falsifiable direction or orientation choice.

source_preferences.reason: The source holds the authored prompts and closures used by this route.

when_not_suitable: Do not turn the elicitation into quantitative force, induction, orbit-radius, or motional-emf practice without governed relations.
